meta.outcome: Additional housing units authorized by building permit over five years (2026-2030), relative to a current-rules baseline forecast by a county permit model, computed per county and summed to the state. Also reported by year: construction starts and homes completed, from Survey of Construction timing curves.
meta.how_to_read: Each parameter has a low_case, central and high_case value. The low estimate uses every low_case value together and the high estimate every high_case value, so the range is wide on purpose. low_case is always the value that gives the smaller effect. basis says whether a value comes from a study, the challenge rules, or a team assumption. Team assumptions should be revisited first.
meta.status: First-pass evidence-anchored assumptions, set 2026-11-15. Values marked basis=assumption are judgment calls anchored to the cited studies, not estimates from them.

implementation_share.label: Share of the state where local governments implement the reform fully
implementation_share.rationale: California's parking and ADU preemptions drew supportive, strategically supportive and resistant local responses, so a state law does not take full effect everywhere. No study gives a statewide share; 0.5-1.0 brackets partial to full compliance.

ramp.label: Share of the full annual effect reached in years 1-5
ramp.unit: share of full effect, by year
ramp.rationale: Early ADU and SB 9 uptake was slow and grew over several years; Auckland's permits roughly doubled within five years rather than at once.

exposure.rationale: Each county is weighted by how much of its housing the reform touches compared with the U.S. as a whole (ACS 2020-2024): single-family detached share for ADUs and missing middle, share of homes in 5+ unit buildings for transit-oriented density and parking. Weights are bounded to 0.25-2.5 so a handful of unusual counties can't dominate a state. This is a team assumption about exposure, not a measured elasticity.

scenarios.label: Scenario 1: Accessory dwelling units
scenarios.benchmark: One detached or semi-detached ADU of at least 600 sq ft allowed on parcels with existing single-family homes; no additional parking required.
scenarios.formula: for each permit-issuing county: ADU rate per 100,000 residents x (population / 100,000) x county weight (single-family detached share vs. U.S.); summed over counties, x (1 - legalization share) x implementation share x ramp[y]

adu_rate_per_100k.label: ADU permits per 100,000 residents per year once the law is in force
adu_rate_per_100k.rationale: Pew: cities under permissive ADU laws issued 81 permits per 100,000 residents in 2025, 26 outside California. Central is set nearer the non-California rate because most states lack California's decade of ADU reforms. These are gross rates in cities of 100,000+, so they likely overstate small-town and rural uptake.

legalization_share.label: Share of ADU permits that legalize an existing unit rather than add a new one
legalization_share.rationale: Permits can legalize units that already exist, and a permitted ADU is not always occupied long-term housing. No study gives a share; 0-30% is a judgment bracket.

data_gaps: Census permits don't separate ADUs, so the state's current ADU rate can't be netted out. If the state already allows ADUs widely, the true increase is smaller.
Parcel counts and lot sizes aren't modeled; the per-capita rate weighted by each county's single-family share stands in for eligible lots.

scenarios.label: Scenario 2: Missing middle (2-6 units)
scenarios.benchmark: 2-6 dwelling units allowed on parcels currently restricted to single-family use, up to three stories; setbacks and lot coverage assumed not to bind.
scenarios.formula: for each county: baseline permit forecast for year y x county weight (single-family detached share vs. U.S.); summed over counties, x missing-middle uplift x implementation share x ramp[y]

mm_uplift.label: Increase in total permits once the reform is fully in effect
mm_uplift.rationale: Low: SB 9 produced few units early on. Central: modest, in line with the small average U.S. response (+0.8% of stock in 3-9 years). High: Lower Hutt's broad upzoning raised net regional starts 12-17%. Auckland's doubling of permits is treated as beyond the range because it was a larger, metro-wide reform.

data_gaps: Uplift applies to each county's permits weighted by its single-family share, not to individual single-family parcels; parcel data aren't included yet.
Financial feasibility by market isn't modeled; weak markets will see less.

scenarios.label: Scenario 3: Transit-oriented density
scenarios.benchmark: Higher allowed residential density (height and/or FAR) near major transit stops; parking requirements may be reduced.
scenarios.formula: for each county: baseline permit forecast for year y x county weight (share of homes in 5+ unit buildings vs. U.S.); summed over counties, x share of permits near major transit x uplift near transit x implementation share x ramp[y]

tod_share_near_transit.label: Share of the state's permits that fall within the transit-proximity threshold
tod_share_near_transit.rationale: Placeholder until stop locations are added: no clean-license national stop dataset has been found yet. Replace with a state-specific share computed from GTFS stops and permit locations.

tod_uplift_near_transit.label: Increase in permits within transit areas once fully in effect
tod_uplift_near_transit.unit: share of permits in transit areas
tod_uplift_near_transit.rationale: Low: Chicago found no detectable increase in permitting within five years, and LA's TOC raised proposals but not permits. High: big NYC upzonings added over 4,000 units in four years. Sao Paulo's corridor reform raised citywide stock 1.6% in the long run.

data_gaps: No major-transit-stop definition or locations yet (see research/data/README.md, open gaps).
Whether current zoning near stops already allows the density isn't modeled.

scenarios.label: Scenario 4: Parking requirement reduction
scenarios.benchmark: Minimum parking requirements reduced or eliminated for new residential development; developers still provide parking where the market demands it.
scenarios.formula: for each county: baseline permit forecast for year y x county weight (share of homes in 5+ unit buildings vs. U.S.); summed over counties, x parking uplift x implementation share x ramp[y]

parking_uplift.label: Increase in total permits once fully in effect
parking_uplift.rationale: Developer-provided parking: about 70% of Seattle projects without a minimum still built some, and responses depend on local demand, so minimums often don't bind (low = 0). A simulation found parking norms cut housing stock about 1.2% in the long run, and a 2025 event study reports supply gains after reforms but no coefficient yet.

data_gaps: Parking costs and the share of projects where minimums bind aren't modeled directly.
Effects overlap with TOD and missing-middle reforms; don't add them.

scenarios.label: Scenario 5: Development fee reduction
scenarios.benchmark: Total development fees (planning, environmental review, building and impact fees) cut 50% across all major categories, from an assumed $50,000 per unit to $25,000.
scenarios.formula: for each county: baseline permit forecast for year y; summed over counties, x fee-cut uplift x ramp[y]

fee_uplift.label: Increase in total permits from a $25,000 per-unit fee cut once fully in effect
fee_uplift.rationale: High: halving development charges made about 5% more projects financially viable in CMHC's model; viability is an upper bound on starts. Low: part of a fee cut is absorbed by land prices, and some fees fund infrastructure that enables building. The $50,000 starting fee is the challenge's assumption, not observed data.

data_gaps: Actual local fee levels aren't used; California LIHTC projects averaged close to $20,000 per unit, well below the $50,000 benchmark.
Implementation share isn't applied because the benchmark cuts fees across all categories statewide.
